prose.summary: An executive assistant runs the operating system around one or two executives: the calendar, the inbox triage, the travel, the pre-reads for board meetings. What separates it from an office administrator role is scope, you are managing someone's judgment about where their time goes, not just their logistics, and increasingly you are running small projects and vendor relationships on their behalf.
prose.day_to_day: Monday usually starts with rebuilding the calendar against what happened over the weekend, since executives take calls on planes and change their minds in transit. You draft agendas, chase three people for the same signature, and reconcile an expense report that's missing two receipts. A good chunk of the week is solo, heads-down in Excel or a slide deck, but the rest is fielding interruptions: someone needs a room booked in twenty minutes, someone else needs to know if the CEO is free Thursday. The moment people in this job wait for is the pre-brief right before a big meeting, when you walk your executive through the room (who's likely to push back, what the numbers say, what to skip if time runs short) and watch it land clean. By Friday you're usually closing out a travel itinerary for the following week and clearing whatever slipped from Monday's list.
prose.work_environment: Most of this work happens in an office, close enough to the executive's door to catch them between calls, which is part of why remote share sits at 24 percent: the job depends on physical proximity and reading a room in real time. Hours track the executive's calendar more than a fixed shift, so a week with an offsite or an earnings call runs long and a quiet week runs normal. Travel comes in bursts tied to board cycles or conferences rather than on a steady schedule. Bad weeks are the ones where two urgent things land at once, a last-minute trip and a deck due the same afternoon, and there's no way to sequence around it.
prose.getting_in: Most postings (61 percent) list a degree as required and another 19 percent prefer one, but 10 percent waive it outright in favor of demonstrated experience, usually two to three years supporting a manager or running an office. The median experience asked for is 3 years, and that's the step where people stall: entry-level assistant roles are easy to find, but the jump to executive-level support wants a track record of handling someone's calendar and correspondence with real judgment, not just administrative competence. Certifications in project management or Excel help on paper but rarely replace that track record. The fastest real path is two years in a coordinator or administrative role at a company with visible executives, followed by a lateral move into an EA seat once you can point to specific meetings you ran or trips you saved from falling apart.
prose.ladder: The first step up is moving from supporting one manager to supporting someone whose calendar has real consequences attached, a VP or C-suite executive where a missed flight or a badly prepped meeting costs something visible. From there you start carrying small projects outright: an offsite budget, a vendor contract, an onboarding process for new hires on the team. The ladder forks around the three-to-five year mark, one branch toward chief of staff or business operations roles that trade calendar work for strategy work, the other toward staying hands-on as an EA to increasingly senior people, which pays well without ever losing the scheduling core of the job.
prose.suits: People who come alive in this job like being the person who already knows the answer when someone panics, the one who has the backup flight booked before the first one gets cancelled. It rewards people who enjoy holding a lot of moving pieces in their head at once and get a genuine charge out of a day that closes with nothing dropped. The people who leave usually wanted to own outcomes rather than enable someone else's, and they're happier once they move into the analyst or project management roles where the work has their name on it instead of their executive's.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume the job is mostly typing and calendar clicks, but a good EA is doing quiet risk management: catching the double-booking before it happens, knowing which emails need an answer in ten minutes versus which can wait a day. Another common assumption is that it's a stepping stone with no ceiling of its own; in practice, senior EA roles at the top of the range pay close to entry-level business analyst salaries and carry real project ownership, not just scheduling.
prose.who_qualifies: Business analysts show the highest overlap (62 percent match), since both roles run on structured reporting and stakeholder juggling, though analysts usually have to relearn the real-time interruption handling that EA work demands. Event planners (56 percent) and customer support specialists (49 percent) also transfer well, the former bringing vendor and logistics experience, the latter bringing the instinct for staying calm while someone else is not. What doesn't transfer automatically from any of these is the judgment call of managing someone else's priorities as if they were your own, that gets built on the job.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows how much of the job is reading a person, not a process, since every executive wants their calendar, inbox, and interruptions handled differently and the postings can't capture that fit. It also can't measure the trust curve: how long it takes before an executive lets you answer email in their voice, which is usually the real marker of seniority in this role.

steps.do: Take an administrative or coordinator role
steps.how: Look for postings at companies with visible senior leadership, even if the title is just 'office coordinator' or 'admin assistant.' This stage runs 1 to 2 years and you're done with it once you've managed a calendar with real conflicts and handled travel booking without supervision.

steps.do: Build fluency in Excel and presentation tools
steps.how: Scheduling and Excel show up in 28 and 23 percent of postings respectively, so get comfortable building a clean pivot table and a board-ready slide deck from a messy data dump. A few weeks of deliberate practice, building three or four sample decks and trackers, is usually enough to stop being the bottleneck on formatting.

steps.do: Take on a small project outright
steps.how: Ask to own something bounded: an offsite, an onboarding checklist, a vendor renewal. This usually happens naturally in year two of an admin role, and you know you're ready to move up once you can describe a project's budget, timeline, and outcome without your manager's help.

steps.do: Move into an EA seat at 2 to 3 years
steps.how: Apply once you have a concrete story: a specific executive you supported, a specific crisis you handled (a cancelled flight, a last-minute board request), and numbers if you have them. This step is where the market gates hardest, since the median years asked is 3, so a resume with less than that needs a strong project story to compensate.

steps.do: Decide: chief of staff track or senior EA
steps.how: Around the three-to-five year mark, choose whether to push toward chief of staff or operations roles (which want a business analyst or project management credential) or stay in EA work supporting increasingly senior executives. Either path takes another 1 to 2 years to establish once chosen.

prose.tools: Scheduling software and Excel are the real gatekeepers, showing up in 28 and 23 percent of postings, since almost every interview will test your ability to manage a complex calendar and build a working spreadsheet under time pressure. Presentation tools (22 percent) matter nearly as much for board and leadership decks. Project management platforms like Jira show up in a smaller but growing share of postings (7 percent), suggesting the role is absorbing more structured project tracking rather than staying purely calendar and correspondence work.

industries.name: Finance and banking
industries.note: Formal, hierarchical, heavy on compliance paperwork and travel for client meetings; calendars are dense and precision matters more than flexibility.

industries.name: Tech and startups
industries.note: Faster pace, less formality, more likely to hand you project ownership early since the org itself is still figuring out its own processes.

industries.name: Manufacturing and supply chain
industries.note: Executives split time between office and plant floor, so travel coordination and supply-chain literacy (22 percent of postings ask for it) matter more here than elsewhere.

industries.name: Professional services
industries.note: Client-facing polish counts for a lot; you're often coordinating across partners and external clients rather than just internal staff.

specializations.name: Chief of staff track
specializations.why: Companies increasingly promote senior EAs into chief of staff roles that carry strategy and operations work; it's worth pursuing if you want ownership of outcomes rather than just calendars.

specializations.name: Event and offsite planning
specializations.why: Event planning shows up in 10 percent of postings and is one of the cleanest lateral moves (28 percent match) if you enjoy the project side of the job more than the daily scheduling grind.

specializations.name: Operations-focused EA (Lean/Six Sigma)
specializations.why: A small but real share of postings (7 percent) ask for process-improvement credentials, useful for EAs who want to formalize the operational side of the role and move toward business operations roles later.

pros: You get a front-row view of how real decisions get made, since you're in the room or on the thread for nearly everything your executive touches.
The work has a clean daily win: a calendar that holds, a trip that goes smoothly, a meeting that starts on time with the right people prepped.
The role compounds; senior EA salaries at the top of the range rival entry-level analyst pay without requiring a career switch.
You build a genuinely transferable skill set (scheduling, stakeholder management, project coordination) that opens doors into operations, recruiting, and business analysis later.
cons: Your schedule bends to someone else's, so a call that runs long or a trip that gets moved up eats into your evening without much notice.
The work is largely invisible when it goes well, people only notice the one time something slips.
Career progression depends partly on the executive you support; a role with a stagnant executive can stall your own growth even if you're doing everything right.
The interruption load is constant, and it takes real practice to stay accurate on detail work (numbers, names, dates) while being pulled in three directions at once.

faq.q: how long does it take to become an executive assistant
faq.a: Most people spend 1 to 2 years in an administrative or coordinator role before moving into an EA seat, since the median experience employers ask for is 3 years. Getting there faster usually means finding a smaller company willing to hand you calendar ownership earlier.

faq.q: can you become an executive assistant without a degree
faq.a: Yes, 10 percent of postings waive the degree requirement outright, and employers in those cases look for 2 to 3 years of hands-on administrative experience instead. That said, 61 percent still list a degree as required, so a no-degree path narrows your options rather than closing them.

faq.q: executive assistant vs office manager, what's the difference
faq.a: An office manager runs the physical and operational side of a workspace (supplies, facilities, sometimes HR logistics) while an executive assistant is dedicated to one or two people's time and priorities. The two roles overlap in smaller companies but diverge sharply once a company grows past a certain size and each becomes its own full-time job.

faq.q: is executive assistant a good career right now
faq.a: It holds up well: the switch rate is 5.6 percent a year, meaning most people who take the role stay in it or move up rather than leaving the field entirely. The pay range (mid-career median around $73k) and clear paths into operations or chief of staff roles make it a reasonable long-term bet if you like the daily rhythm of the work.

faq.q: can an executive assistant work remotely
faq.a: Some can, remote share sits at 24 percent, but the job leans in-person because so much of the value is reading a room and being physically available when something urgent comes up. Fully remote EA roles tend to support executives who themselves work remotely or across distributed teams.
